translations.text: The life and conduct of the holy Apa Eustathius.

The military commander of Emperor Trajan, together with Theopiste his wife and Agapius and Theopistus his sons, who completed their struggle in the great city of Rome on the twentieth day of the month of Thoth, under Emperor Trajan. In peace. Amen.
A place of instruction is provided for holy people,
which belongs partly to nature and partly to free choice, both together,
achieving virtue and wishing to instruct those near him through the others who lived from the beginning,
those who receive favor from him, who has done good to us all from the beginning, our God and our Lord Jesus Christ,
these things that he commands and requires of us.
I am speaking of acts of gratitude.
We are those to whom he does good, and our establishment [?]. Moreover, many are the teachings and deeds of the courageous and blessed people that are set down for us in the holy Scriptures,
like images that have a soul, so that those who wish to follow them may imitate their honorable achievements and, through their own courage, not prove inferior to them.
For my part, those about whom I am now going to write to you are people who achieved virtue in our own times and are not inferior in their achievements and their courage
to the people of old about whom the holy Scriptures were written, so that those who hear may love what is good and may themselves turn
to the strength of their virtues—those who say, “It is impossible to achieve virtue now, in these last times.”
But I say that, for anyone who wants to do good,
the hardship of the times and a harsh way of living cannot prevent a life determined to accomplish good deeds.
If someone wishes first to follow the reasoning of nature and the teachings of the holy people of whom we have spoken,
he will find ease on the path of a life full of virtue, after the example of those who are now set before me.
Let us speak about them and write to you about the beginning of their life and the [?] of the honor of their course, through the things that happened to us.
Let us make them known, and you yourselves should listen to them willingly, without any unbelief
or hesitation, O blessed people and servants of Christ.
Now it happened during the reign of Emperor Trajan, when idol worship was widespread, that there rose to power
a military commander named Placidus. He was close to the emperor and was especially honored for his ancestry by this world's standards. He was also extremely wealthy,
surpassing all the dignitaries of the palace in possessions, gold and silver, numerous slaves, and other property.
He was a pagan in his religion, but he was adorned with righteous deeds.
He used to help those in distress.
He helped those who were being treated unjustly, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry.
He also rescued many who were being condemned to death, using his own money.
In short, he provided for everyone in need according to their bodily needs.
He became a new Cornelius at that time.
He had a wife, and she too worshiped idols.
But she adorned herself with every good deed in this same way.
They had two sons.
They raised these too in the same way, in keeping with their good intentions.
The man was very well known for the good deeds he did.
He was also famous for his strength, so that the barbarians were afraid when they merely heard his name, because he was a very great warrior.
He distinguished himself in every battle.
His whole enthusiasm was devoted solely to hunting wild animals and excelling at it.
But God, who is good and loves all people everywhere who are worthy of him, did not forget that man's good deeds.
Nor did he wish to let his good disposition perish.
Rather, as it is written, “In every nation, whoever fears the Lord and practices righteousness is accepted by him.”
Since he had such a compassionate heart, God was pleased to save him in the following way, which we will relate.
One day he went out, as was his custom, to hunt wild animals in the mountains.
He went with his army, and all his servants were with him.
A herd of deer appeared before him, grazing.
He ordered his army to pursue them.
While the whole body of soldiers was occupied with catching the animals,
one of them appeared, and it was beautiful.
and taller than all the others. It separated from the herd and came out.
It ran into the wooded places in the rugged mountains, where it was difficult to walk.
When Placidus saw it,
he wanted to catch it.
He took some soldiers with him, left all the rest behind, and chased after it.
But those who had gone with him grew tired and gave up, while he pressed on alone in pursuit.
By God's providence, however, he did not grow tired, nor did the horse he was riding give up in the rugged terrain.
After he had spent a long time chasing it, he found himself far from his army.
Then that animal stood on a very high mountain.
When the general approached it, with no one beside him, he stood looking in every direction.
And he considered how he could catch it.
And God, who loves humanity, who [?] the salvation of people in many ways,
had this man caught in his trap, like Cornelius through Peter, and like Paul, to whom he appeared while Paul was pursuing him.
After a long time had passed, while Placidus stood looking at the animal and marveling at the beauty of its great size,
and wondering how he could catch it, the Lord showed him a sign of this kind, so that he could see him.
He appeared to him in this way:
There was a sign of a cross between its antlers,
shining more brightly than the sun.
There between its antlers he also bore the likeness of the body that God had assumed in the Virgin's womb,
and had placed upon the cross for our salvation.
He called to Placidus in a human voice from the animal, saying,
"Placidus, why are you chasing me?
For it is for your sake that I have appeared to you through this animal.
For I am Jesus, whom you serve without knowing him.
The acts of kindness that you perform have come before me.
That is why I have revealed myself to you,
and have ensnared you through this irrational animal,
and caught you in the nets of my divinity.
It is not right for those who honor me through their good deeds to be slaves to unclean demons and to dead, mute, and unfeeling idols."
This is why I came down to earth in the form in which you see me, wanting to save the human race.
When Placidus heard these things, he was afraid and fell to the ground.
After a long time had passed, he got up by himself, wanting to understand exactly the wonder that had appeared.
He said, “What, then, is this vision that I have seen?
And what kind of voice is this that I have heard?
Reveal yourself to me, you who are speaking with me, for I believe in you.”
The Lord said to him, “Pay attention, Placidus.
I am Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, who created heaven and earth when they did not exist.
I created all matter, which is beyond counting.
I am the one who made the light appear and separated it from the darkness.
I am the one who created the sun to give light during the day.
And I appointed the moon and the stars to give light at night.
I am the one who appointed the times, the seasons, and the days.
I am the one who formed the human being from the earth.
I appeared on earth in the flesh that I took on for the salvation of humankind.
I am the one who was crucified. I died and was buried, and on the third day I rose from the dead.”
When Placidus heard these things, he fell on his face and cried out, “I believe, Lord, that you are the one who created everything and who brings back those who stray and those who have gone astray.
And you are the one who brings those who have died back to life.”
The Lord answered, “If you believe, go and make your way to the chief priests of the Christians, and seek through them the grace that comes through baptism.”
Placidus answered him, “Lord, give me permission to tell these things to my wife and my children, so that they too may believe in you.”
The Lord said to him, “Tell them.
And let all of you be cleansed of defilement by receiving the seal of baptism. Then return to this place, so that I may reveal myself to you and tell you the mystery of salvation.”
Then Placidus came down from the mountain.
He went into his house.
When evening came, he began telling his wife and his children what he had seen in the vision and how the Lord had appeared to him.
His wife immediately cried out, “My lord, my brother, you have seen the God who was crucified, the one whom the Christians worship!”
For he alone is the true God, who saves those who put their hope in him.
And she cried out very loudly, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord Jesus Christ, and on my other two children.”
And she said to her husband, “Last night I too saw him, and he said to me, ‘Tomorrow you, your husband, and your children will come to me.’

And I recognized that he was God, Jesus Christ, the God of the Galileans. He wishes to reveal himself to you through such a miracle, by means of an animal, so that you will be amazed at his power and believe in him.
Come now, then, while it is night. Let us go and receive baptism from the high priests of the Christians, just as he commanded you.
For through this, those who believe in him become members of his household.”
Placidus answered and said, “This is what the one who appeared to me told me.”
At midnight they secretly took their two children and a few of their slaves.
They went to the high priest of the Christians and told him the whole vision.
They professed their belief in the Lord Jesus Christ.
They begged him to give them the seal of Christ through baptism.
He rejoiced and gave glory to God, who wishes everyone to live and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
The high priest received them, instructed them, and entrusted them with the holy mysteries
of the faith. And he baptized them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
He named Placidus Eustathius, and his wife Theopiste. As for his children, he named the older one Agapius and the younger one Theopistus.
He gave them a share of the precious body and blood of Christ and sent them away,
saying to them, “May God, Christ, be with you,
and may he grant you his kingdom forever.
Know that the hand of the Lord is with you.
And I urge you, when you are in paradise, to remember the soul of John, this least and poorest one.”
When morning came, Eustathius took some horses.
He went to the mountain and approached the place where he had seen the vision.
He sent the soldiers of the hunting party to hunt the animals.
But he himself stayed alone for a little while.
Afterward he went on his way.
He approached the place where he had first seen the figure.
He fell on his face and cried out, saying, “Lord, I have realized that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, and I have believed in you, your good Father, and the Holy Spirit.
Now, therefore, I beg you:
If you have made me worthy of the holy grace of your divinity, explain to me the things you told me.”
Immediately the Lord answered him, saying, “Blessed are you, Placidus, because you have received the cleansing of grace.
You have clothed yourself in incorruptibility, which lasts forever.
Now, therefore, the work of your faith has become evident.
For the devil will envy you because you have left him behind,
and he will make every effort to use every trick to fight against you.
For you must bear many trials.
If you endure them, you will receive the crown of victory.
Look, until now you have risen very high in worldly affairs and temporary wealth.
Now become rich also in spiritual greatness.
Do not grow weak now or lose heart over the glory of this world that you formerly possessed.
But just as you proved yourself a mighty man among people, fighting and striving to please a mortal king,
so strive in the same way to be a mighty man against the devil, and keep the faith for me.
I am the immortal King.
For you must become a new Job in these times, one who will defeat the devil through trial.
Watch yourself, lest a blasphemous thought arise in your heart.
But when you have been humbled, I will come to you and restore your former glory.”
And when the Lord had said these things to him,
he ascended into heaven,
while saying to him, “Eustathius, be ready and willing for the trial appointed for you in the last days.”

And Eustathius said, “If this is the end of my days, I beg you, my Lord: if it is impossible for the things you have now decreed against me to pass me by without happening to me, give the command to take our trial upon yourself.
But give us strength, Lord God of hosts, for it is you in whom we trust.”
The Lord said to him, “Keep up the struggle, Eustathius. My grace will guard your hearts.”
Then Saint Eustathius came down from the mountain.
He went to his house and told his wife what the Lord had said to him.
They knelt down together.
They prayed, saying, “Lord, let your will be done.”
A few days later, a plague broke out in his house, and all his servants died.
When this happened, Eustathius recognized the trial, just as he had been warned beforehand that it would happen to him. He accepted it joyfully and encouraged his wife not to lose heart.
A short time later, his horses and all his livestock died.
In the same way, he accepted this further trial with joy.
After this, he left his house with his wife and children, without anyone knowing.
He withdrew to another place.
When the criminals learned that they had gone away, they hurried there at night and plundered his house.
They left absolutely nothing behind, whether gold, silver, or clothing.
After all these losses and sorrows, they were stripped of all their wealth and everything they owned.
All these things happened through the plotting of the adversary.
On that day, all the people were celebrating and rejoicing over their victory against the Persians.
The emperor was celebrating with them with great pomp.
Eustathius, too, should have been celebrating with them,
since he was a high-ranking general in the Roman Senate. The emperor looked for him but did not find him.
When the emperor learned that, in a single hour, nothing at all had been left to him of everything he owned,
and that neither he nor those with him could be found,
the emperor and the entire Senate were deeply grieved over him.
They were astonished at what had happened to him.
Then his wife said to him, “How long are we going to stay here?
Get up, and let us take the children who are left to us and go away. Let us leave this country behind, because we have become a laughingstock to those who know us.”
That night, they took their children and set out for Egypt.
After traveling for a day or two, they came to the sea.
They found a ship moored in the harbor and asked to board it.
The ship’s captain was a savage barbarian.
When they had boarded the ship, they set sail.
The captain saw that Eustathius’s wife had a very beautiful face, and he fell in love with her.
When he reached the seashore, he demanded his fare from him, but he had nothing to pay with.
So he seized his wife on the pretext of the fare.
For this was the plan he had devised: not to give her back to her husband.
Eustathius spent a long time speaking with him and pleading with him. The captain signaled to his men to seize him and throw him into the sea.
When Eustathius realized what they were plotting, he reluctantly left his wife behind, took his two children, and walked away with them, weeping.
He lamented, saying, “Woe to me, my children! Your mother has been taken away by a barbarian!”
As he walked, he sighed and wept, and he came to a river. Because of the great volume of water in the streams,
he could not carry his two children across at the same time.
He put one on his shoulders.
He left the other on this side of the water.
He crossed the water and left the one he had carried on the far bank.
Then he turned back for the other.
While he was in the middle of the river,
he looked and saw that a lion had snatched his child, picked him up, and gone away.
His father gave him up as lost.
Then he turned back, still holding out hope for the other.
But again he saw that the other had been snatched by a wolf.
When he saw that his children had been carried off by the wild beasts,
he pulled at the hair of his head.
He lamented intensely, in great bitterness.
He set about throwing himself into the sea, all alone.
But God's care strengthened his heart so that he would understand what was going to happen to him.
He did not do this, but crossed the water to go up into the wilderness.
Some shepherds saw the little boy in the lion's mouth, unharmed.
They said plainly, “It is God's providence that is guarding this little boy
and helping him and rescuing him from the wild beast.”
They ran after the lion with their dogs.
The lion became afraid.
By God's arrangement, the lion dropped the little boy.
It ran away, and the shepherds picked up the little boy and raised him as their own son on the eastern side of the river.
As for the other one, whom the wolf had snatched,
God's providence sheltered him from harm.
When some farmers saw him, they ran and took him away from the wolf. It had not hurt him at all.
The farmers and the shepherds lived in the same village.
They took the little children and brought them up in their homes.
But Eustace knew nothing of what had happened.
Instead, he walked along weeping and saying things like this: “Woe to me!
I was once flourishing like a tree.
But now I have dried up and withered.
Woe to me! I was once prosperous, but now I am like a captive. Woe to me! I once had great numbers of soldiers under my command, but now you have left me all alone.
They did not even allow me to keep just my wife and children.
But do not abandon me completely, Lord.
And do not forget my tears.
Lord, you told me, ‘You must be tested like Job.’
And look, I see that my sufferings have become far greater.”
Even if that man was stripped of his possessions, he was allowed a dung heap to sit on.
But I am to live as a wretched stranger, bearing all this suffering.
Job, at least, had his children with him to comfort him
and to suffer with him.
But wild beasts have taken away the comfort of my children from me.

Even if that man's branches were cut off—I mean his children—he could see that the root remained with him, namely his wife, who was a comfort to him, even if, being a woman, she stumbled in something she said.
But as for me, wretched as I am, my root has been torn up on every side.
I see no ray of light from the lamp of my family.
Instead, I am like a tree in the desert, constantly shaken by the devil's windstorm.
No, Lord, do not afflict your servant for being so full of words,
uttering these improper things in my anguish.
Set a guard, then, Lord, over my mouth, and a strong door over my lips, so that my heart will not turn aside to evil words
and you cast me out of your presence. Give me relief, then, Lord.
As he said these things, sighing and weeping, he came upon a village called Bassus.
He went into it and worked there, earning his daily food.
After he had lived there for a long time, the people of that village asked him to go and guard the crops in the fields. He spent ten years doing this and receiving his wages.
His children, meanwhile, were brought up in the village we mentioned earlier, without knowing that they were brothers.
The ship's captain who had taken Eustathius's wife brought her to his homeland.
A great shadow from God overshadowed her, so that the barbarian [?] touch her throughout all that time.
For this was what that woman had asked of God: that he would not let that foreigner touch her at all.
After that barbarian died, she remained in that place.
Some days later, those foreigners among whom Eustathius's wife was living rose up and set out to seize the territory of the Romans.
The emperor Trajan was greatly distressed because of the war with the foreigners.
He remembered Placidus, especially his strength and his many victories over the foreigners.
The memory of Eustathius stirred within him.
He was bewildered by the change that had come over him so suddenly.
So he reviewed his own situation and that of the soldiers in his kingdom with regard to the war.
He was deeply saddened about Placidus. He consulted the soldiers, asking, “Is Placidus still alive?”
He said, “Whoever reports, ‘I have found him,’ I will give him great honor and provisions, and I will make him very rich.”
Two of his soldiers—one named Antiochus and the other Acacius—had served Eustathius continually when he was with them.
They went looking for him and searched almost the entire kingdom until they reached the village where Eustathius was.
As they were walking through the places Eustathius was guarding, he saw them from a distance.
He recognized them by the way they moved as they walked.
He remembered his former way of life and began to grieve.
He prayed, saying, “Lord God, merciful one, who saves everyone who hopes in him, just as I have unexpectedly seen those who used to travel with me,
now, then, please look down on me and your servant, my wife.
For I know that my children have become food for wild beasts because of my evil deeds. Grant that I too may see them at the resurrection.”
While Eustathius was still saying these things, he heard a voice saying to him, “Take courage, Eustathius! In due time
you will be restored to your former position, and you will receive your wife and your children.
At the resurrection of the dead, you will see everlasting blessings.
So do not deny me, and you will find unending rest, and your name will grow greater through all generations.”
When he heard these things, he was afraid and went down from the place where he was.
He stood beside them on the road, facing them.
He recognized them with certainty, but they did not recognize him.
They said to him, “Greetings, friend!” He, in turn,
said to them, “Peace to you, my brothers!”
They said to him, “Do you happen to know this stranger here called Placidus, along with his wife and his children?
If you give us information about him, we will give you a great deal of money.”
He said to them, “Why are you looking for him?”
They said to him, “He is our friend, and we have wanted to meet him for many years.”
He said to them, “I do not know the man.”
“Rest here with me, since it is getting late, and refresh yourselves with me in this place where I am staying.”
“For I too am a stranger.”
And he brought them into his house.
He went to buy some wine for them to drink.
He said to the owner of the house where he was staying, “I know these men.”
“That is why they have come to me here. So give me some food and wine, so that they can refresh themselves here with me. I will pay you for them when I receive my wages.”
The man gladly gave him everything he needed.
Eustathius continued serving them. He could not bear it as he thought about his former life, but he restrained himself from weeping.
He went outside, wept, and washed his face.
He went inside and served them again. And he looked at him again.
Little by little they began to recognize him, and they spoke to one another, saying, “This man looks like the one we are looking for.”
The other said to his companion, “Yes, he looks like him. But I know of a mark on his neck from when he was wounded in the war against the Massagetae.”
“Let us look closely at him to see whether he has this mark or not.”
“If it is on his neck, then he is that man.”
When they looked carefully for the mark, they saw the scar on his neck.
Immediately they rose and kissed him.
They asked him, “Are you Placidus, the man who was once the great general?”
But he denied it, saying, “No,” and restrained himself from weeping.
But when they pointed out the scar on his neck to him, they solemnly insisted, “You are Placidus the general!” They also asked him about his wife and his children.
He said to them, “They have died.”
While he was still talking with them about these things, they raised their voices and wept so loudly that everyone in the village heard them.
While they were still crying out, the villagers came to see what had happened, and they were frightened and distressed.
But the soldiers quieted the disturbance and told them about the man’s valor and his former honor.
When the villagers heard these things, they sighed deeply, saying, “Great is the honor of this man who became our hired laborer!”
Then the soldiers reported the matter to the king, and they dressed him in fine clothes from among those they had with them.
They took him and set off along the road.
Everyone in the village walked with him to see him off.
But he urged them to return and sent them away.
While he was still traveling along the road with the soldiers, he told them what he had seen, how he had seen Christ, and also that he had been named Eustathius.
He told them everything that had happened to him. After they had spent fifteen days traveling along the road, they came to Emperor Trajan.
They told him how they had found Placidas.
Emperor Trajan came out to meet him, embraced him, and wept greatly.
He asked him why he had gone away.
He told Trajan and the entire senate what had happened to him, and about his wife and children.
He also told them how the shipowner had forcibly taken his wife, how his children had been carried off by wild animals, and about their suffering.
In short, they were all filled with great joy because they had found him alive. The emperor comforted him and made him commander of the army again, as before.
When Eustathius inspected the entire army, he realized that it would not be sufficient for the war against the barbarians.
He informed the emperor.
Emperor Trajan ordered recruits to be enlisted.
He wrote a letter to every city, instructing them to enlist men and examine them to see whether they were fit to be made soldiers.
When they went to the village where Eustathius's children were, they enlisted his two sons, who were handed over to them as recruits.
The people of that place testified that they were physically strong and handsome in appearance.
When Eustathius gathered all the recruits, he assigned them to the military units. He saw that the two young men were more handsome than all the others.
He appointed them to his service because he recognized their noble character through their conduct.
In his kindness, he kept them with him. Their eagerness drew them on each day, so that he loved them still more.
He ordered that they should eat with him at his table.
After this, he arranged the troops as he usually did.
He went out to war, and in the territory that the barbarians had seized before that day,
he freed those who had been taken captive there.
He crossed the river called the Hydaspes, which had risen high, and advanced into the interior of the barbarians' territory.
He defeated these others too and plundered the whole country.
Eustathius made plans concerning other matters through the providence of God, who was calling him to go up to the place where his wife was.
She had been protected from the beginning by God's care, as I have said, because of the violence of the ship's captain and tyrant.
When that foreigner died, she quietly withdrew by herself and settled in the garden of one of the people living there.
She made herself a shelter where she lived alone.
When the general had taken that village and plundered it, he pitched his camp there
for three days, resting with his army, since that place was suitable for a rest.
He also stayed in that garden, where his wife was. The two sons, for their part, lodged at their mother's shelter.
When noon came, they sat down and told each other about the events of their childhood.
For they did not know that their mother was in that place, nor did they know what had happened to them.
Their mother was sitting there, listening to what they were saying.
The older brother said to the younger, “I remember nothing from my childhood except this alone: my father was a general,
and my mother was a very beautiful woman. He had two sons.
One was younger than I was, with curly hair and a handsome face.
One night they took us and brought us out of our house.
They took us aboard a ship. I do not know where we were going.
When we reached the shore by ship, my mother remained alone aboard the ship. I do not know why. But our father took the two of us and walked away weeping.
When he came to a river, he crossed it with my younger brother.
But he left me on this side of the water.
As he was about to return to get me, a lion pounced on me, carried me off, and went into the wilderness with me.
Some shepherds were tending sheep in that place. They rescued me from the lion and raised me there.
That is what I know. I do not know what happened to my younger brother and my father.”
As he heard these things from his older brother, he threw himself down and wept. He said, “You are my brother!
For I have realized from what you have said that you are my older brother, because I too was raised by shepherds. They told me, ‘You were rescued from a wolf.’”
He embraced him, and they kissed each other.
While their mother was still listening to these things, she realized that they were her children because of what they had said about her abduction at sea on the ship.
She was saying to herself, “Could these be my children, or not?
Could my children look like this?”
But she was deeply distressed, and her heart was stirred as she watched the young children embracing one another and weeping.
She kept watching them, saying, “Could they be my children? Especially since they said that their father was a general and that their mother had remained on the ship.”
The next day she went to the general and said, “I beg you, my lord, I am a woman from the land of the Romans. I was taken captive and brought here.
So I beg you, take me to my homeland.”
While she was still saying these things, she began to recognize him as her husband by the distinguishing features she knew in him. Once she recognized him, she was afraid to question him.
But when she could no longer restrain herself, she bowed down before him, saying, “I beg you, my lord, do not be angry with me.
For I want you to tell me about your former life, because

I too think that you are Placidus the general, whose name was changed to Eustathius when you were baptized in the name of Christ Jesus, who appeared to you through an animal without the power of speech.
You believed in him, and when you fell into the trials that the Lord had foretold to you, you took your wife, who is myself, and your two sons, Agapius and Theopistus.
You set out for Egypt, and when we reached the sea, we boarded the ship. We cast off, sailed, and put out to sea.
You lost me because of the foreign shipmaster, who seized me.
He took me to his homeland. But the Lord Jesus Christ is my witness that neither that man nor anyone else defiled my body. Rather, I have preserved my chastity until now.
Now, if you are Eustathius, as I have recognized you by the signs I have mentioned to you, I charge you by the power of Christ: tell me, and hide nothing.”
When Eustathius heard these things, he was utterly amazed.
He looked at her features and recognized her, and great joy came over him.
He immediately stood up and embraced her, saying, “I am Eustathius, the one you are speaking of.” And they kissed one another with a spiritual kiss.
They shed many tears and gave glory to God, who always does good to his servants and brings them out of all their troubles.
His wife said to him, “Where are my children?”
Then he said to her, weeping, “Wild beasts carried them off.” And he told her what had happened to them while they were with him.
But she said, “Let us give thanks to the Lord, for perhaps, just as he has graciously restored us to one another, he will also graciously restore our children to us.”
Eustathius said to her, “I have already told you that wild beasts carried them off.”
She answered, “Yesterday, while I was sitting in the garden, I heard two young men talking to one another about their childhood and recounting what had happened to them.
I recognized them as our children. But they did not recognize one another until the older one's words gave the younger one a sign by which to recognize him.”
So, if you have not known this until now, then understand that God's mercy has given us back to one another.
Call them yourself and question them, and they will tell you.
The general called the two boys and asked them, “Whose children are you, and what happened to you in your childhood?”
They in turn told him what had happened to them, and immediately he recognized that they were indeed his children.
He embraced them warmly and kissed them.
Both of them threw their arms around their children's necks.
They wept for an hour and thanked the Lord for their wonderful reunion.
The news of what had happened to them reached all the people of the city.
They gathered in one place, marveling and rejoicing over their reunion,
and even more over the victory against the barbarians. They held a great celebration that day because they had recognized one another.
The next day they called upon the Lord, raising their voices in thanksgiving for his great love for humanity.
After he had plundered the barbarians' territory, they returned with great joy, bringing with them a great quantity of spoils and many captives.
When Eustace returned from the war, Emperor Trajan died.
Another emperor named Hadrian succeeded him. He was exceedingly wicked, more so than all the emperors who had preceded him.
When Eustace returned from the war, the emperor came out to meet him, according to the custom of the Roman emperors.
He brought all his nobles with him to celebrate the victory over all the places he had captured.
The bravery he had learned about, together with the finding of his wife and children, increased his joy even more.
When he entered the city, the emperor went ahead and entered the temple of Apollo. Eustace did not go inside with him but stayed outside.
The emperor summoned him and asked him, “Why did you not come into the temple of Apollo and offer sacrifices to the gods,
now that you have won the victory and returned from the war, and offer them sacrifices of thanksgiving, especially since you have found your wife and children?”
Eustace said to the emperor, “I will offer our supplication and our prayer to my king, Christ Jesus,
together with many prostrations, because he had mercy on my misery and brought us out of captivity.
He is the one who gave me my wife and my children. He helped us just as he had told me before I received baptism in his name.
So now I acknowledge no other god besides him.
For he is God, who created heaven and earth, who alone performs these great wonders.”
Then the king became angry when he heard these things from Eustathius.
He had him brought before him as a pagan, together with his wife and children.
He spoke to them with frightening words and threats.
But the saints paid no attention and were not afraid at all.
When the king saw their fearlessness and their faith in Christ, he ordered them to be taken to the arena and a great lion to be released against them.
When the lion rushed toward them, it stopped beside the saints, bent its knees, and bowed down before them. It also lowered its head toward them.
Afterward it came out of the arena and went away.
When the king saw this great spectacle—that the wild beast had not touched them—he was bewildered.
He ordered a bronze calf to be made so that the saints could be thrown into it and a fire lit beneath them.
The crowd gathered to watch the saints’ struggle and the spectacle.
As they were being brought out by means of the mechanisms of the torture device to be thrown into it,
the blessed Eustathius begged the executioners to let them pray.
He stretched out his hands, together with his wife and children.
They prayed, saying, “Lord, God of hosts, whom no one sees, but whom we have seen according to his will,
hear us now as we cry out to you. Bring our prayer to fulfillment for us, with one mind, in the confession of your name and your holy faith.
Make us worthy to be counted among the holy martyrs, like the three holy young boys, [?] tested by fire, who did not deny you.
In the same way, accept us too in this fire as a sacrifice pleasing to you, as we also become a burnt offering in the fire.
Lord, grant grace and a spiritual gift to our bodies, so that everyone who remembers us may receive a spiritual gift in the kingdom of heaven, and also rest upon the earth.
Even if they are in danger at sea or on rivers, if they call upon your holy name, save them from their danger.
If those burdened with many sins bow down before you in our name, forgive them their sins. And everyone who commemorates us on the day bearing our name—be their helper, Lord.
Let the threatening fire surrounding us become refreshing dew for us, so that, Lord, our bodies may not be destroyed in it.”
As they said these things in prayer, they heard a voice from heaven saying, “Just as you have been mighty champions in this life
and have endured many trials, now do not be afraid. Come up here in peace and receive the imperishable crown.
Enjoy forever the good things prepared for you, in return for the sufferings you experienced
and the trials you endured for a short time.”
When the saints heard these things, they willingly handed themselves over, and the soldiers threw them into the bronze instrument.
When they had thrown them in, the flame of the fire surrounded them, and they gave glory to the holy Trinity, to whom victory belongs.
After a little while, they placed their souls in God's hands. The fire did not touch their bodies at all, nor even the hair of their heads.
After three days, the ungodly emperor Hadrian came to the place where the saints had met their end.
He ordered them to open the bronze bull so that he could see what had happened to the saints.
When they opened it, they found the bodies of the saints intact, with no damage to them. They thought they were alive.
When they brought them out, they laid them on the ground. Great fear and amazement seized everyone standing around them, and the bodies of the saints shone like snow.
When the defiled Hadrian saw them, he was amazed and afraid, and he withdrew.
The crowd standing there also cried out, saying, “You are great, Lord, God of the Christians!
You are the great and only true God, Jesus Christ, and there is no other besides you, for you did not allow evil to touch the bodies of the saints.
Instead, they became still more radiant, shining exceedingly brightly in glory and joy.”
When evening came, the Christians came and took the bodies of the holy martyrs. They secretly placed them in an honored place in the city of Rome.
And after the persecution [?], they built a shrine for them, celebrating in it with hymns and songs of praise according to the custom of the Christians.
They commemorate [?] the holy repose of these honored martyrs on the twentieth day of the month of December, which is Thoth in the language of the Egyptians.
This is the life and struggle of these blessed holy martyrs:
Saint Apa Eustathius, Apa Agapius and Apa Theopistus, his sons, and Amma Theopiste, his wife.
This is the completion of their honored struggle.
Everyone, then, who is worthy of their holy commemoration and calls upon them will obtain the good things of the kingdom of heaven through the grace
and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom glory belongs to him, together with his good Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever.
Amen.
Victor [?], the least deacon, son of Macarius, [?] deacon.
